A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AM-µP effective-depth scaling work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original learning-rate sweeps, fitted depth exponents, and ablations for CNNs, ResNets, and vision Transformers on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and an ImageNet subset.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds width/epoch robustness results, direct zero-shot depth-transfer comparisons, and a preliminary audio-classification sweep in Appendix E.4.

M1.justification: The arithmetic-mean update budget, initialization rules, architecture-specific depth counts, and L^(-3/2) learning-rate transfer procedure are retained. Expanded explanations of effective depth and stronger Transformer proof assumptions do not introduce a different algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix E.4 adds an evaluated audio-classification scenario beyond the retained vision datasets. This is a limited, four-depth preliminary extension; the audio dataset and model are not identified. Additional ViT widths and epochs remain within existing task coverage.

E2.justification: The new direct-transfer experiment compares theory-scaled learning rates against unchanged source-rate transfer, using independently tuned target rates as oracle references. The existing PathSum comparison in Figure 3 is retained.

E3.justification: Appendix E.4 introduces a substantive source-to-target transfer evaluation: calibrate at block depth D0=12, compare scaled and unscaled transfer with independently tuned target rates under a three-epoch budget, and measure log-LR error and training loss. It also adds widths 288/384/480, epoch-1–3 selection, and R² reporting. These are additional protocols; the original one-epoch benchmark protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds sensitivity checks for ViT proxy width and the epoch used to select learning rates, including a noisier smallest-width epoch-3 fit. Existing optimizer, activation, normalization, dropout, padding, kernel-size, and loss-landscape analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds, depth-wise 95% confidence intervals for log10 learning rates, and inverse-variance weighted least squares. No changed run counts or new uncertainty-estimation procedure are reported. Added R² values describe fit quality.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 add substantive new results while Tables 1 and 3 retain their scores. The new transfer experiment reports median log-LR error decreasing from 0.314 for raw transfer to 0.057 for scaled transfer; Table 5 shows depth-6 losses of 1.780 versus 1.768. Additional results include width/epoch fits and an audio slope of -1.578 with R²=0.891. Appendix E.3 also corrects the printed kernel-ablation slopes to negative values.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3–D.4 replaces branch isotropy and the bounded single-layer LayerNorm argument with an explicit assumption about composed Jacobians: uniformly bounded tangent-overlap propagation, vanishing remainders, and controlled fluctuations. The proposition, depth-scaling proof, and pre-norm extension are revised accordingly. This substantially changes the conditions supporting the Transformer theorem, although its exponent and the CNN/ResNet derivations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion qualify the universal optimal-learning-rate framing as a shared leading-order base learning-rate scale for the studied dense architecture families. The -3/2 law and calibration-and-transfer contribution remain central; v2 more clearly separates this claim from full-schedule optimality.

C2.justification: New Section 6 explains initialization-only scope, later-training dependence, transfer within optimizer/schedule families, and architectural cases potentially requiring different depth coefficients. The experimental discussion emphasizes finite-depth offsets, and Appendix D discusses LayerNorm null directions and the assumed stable propagation regime. These add substantive applicability boundaries absent from v1's broader presentation.

D1.justification: Appendix E.4 supplies concrete settings for the new checks, including proxy widths, source block depth 12, source LR 2.462×10^-3, and the three-epoch transfer budget. No new code-access or hardware information appears, and the audio dataset, architecture, and detailed protocol remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Bordelon et al. (2023), Stable ResNet, Hayou's width-transfer proof, and MoE hyperparameter-transfer work. Related work distinguishes these settings and attributes residual depth-transfer results to Bordelon et al. (2023), while retaining Bordelon and Pehlevan (2025) for deep-linear analysis. The overall research position remains similar.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory framing, related-work discussion, depth-convention explanation, experimental interpretation, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting around the base-rate and leading-order distinction. Dedicated limitations and impact sections are added. Author order and publication-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4–6, corrects the sign convention in Table 3's caption, and relocates existing floats as text expands. Existing plotted content is retained, including all embedded figure images; the overall two-column layout is unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 provides direct empirical support for transfer beyond v1's fitted scaling curves and states more useful limitations. Appendix D replaces an unsupported inference from bounded individual Jacobians with explicit composed-propagation conditions, improving transparency at the cost of a stronger, unverified assumption. The gains are limited by short training budgets, sparse documentation of the new checks, and several unresolved citation markers. Overall, the evidence and claim calibration improve, without establishing substantially broader validity.
